# Systematic Review: The Psychosocial Impacts of Autism-Related Genetic Testing

**Authors:** Ben C. Wills; Margaret M. Matthews; Josephine Johnston; Isabel Bolo; Ruth Ottman; Paul S. Appelbaum

**Affiliations:** aUniversity of California San Diego, La Jolla, California | bAt the time of the study: The Hastings Center, Garrison, New York | cAt the time of the study: Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia | dHarvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts | eUniversity of Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand | fAt the time of the study:Columbia University, New York, New York | gColumbia University, New York, New York | hNew York State Psychiatric Institute, New York, New York

## Abstract

To perform a systematic literature review of the psychosocial impacts on parents and autistic people of receiving autism-related genetic test results.

Systematic searches of MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science Core Collection, Sociological Index, and Scopus were conducted for articles appearing through October 27, 2024. The authors screened 3,606 articles. The quality of the included articles was assessed with the QuADS appraisal tool.

Twenty-two articles met inclusion criteria. Across research and clinical settings, articles assessed impacts of receiving actual (n=18) or hypothetical (n=4) genetic test results. Twenty articles assessed impacts on parents and prospective parents, while two assessed impacts on autistic adults. Psychological impacts of receiving results varied and included relief, peace of mind, reduced guilt, disappointment, fear, frustration, stress, blame, and guilt. Comparison of the frequencies of these responses was limited by heterogeneous assessment methods, variable reporting formats, and inconsistent outcome measures across studies. Receiving results sometimes confirmed diagnoses, led to altered care plans, influenced family planning, or impacted the decision to end or continue a pregnancy. Most articles reported low-to-mild or highly variable satisfaction with the testing experience. Studies of autistic adults reported strong concerns about testing without consent and discriminatory uses of genetics.

Impacts on parents and prospective parents appear relatively modest, albeit with mixed valences—a finding broadly similar to return-of-results studies for other complex genetic conditions. Although the findings of the two studies of autistic adults differ substantially, they suggest that autistic people and current and prospective parents of autistic children may have significantly different experiences and perspectives. Clinicians should recognize these differences and help parents understand and weigh them in decision-making.

## Abstract

We systematically searched for articles on the impacts of receiving genetic test results about autism. Our search returned 22 studies that varied widely. Seventeen focused on parents/caregivers of autistic children, three on the prenatal context, and two on autistic adults. Psychological impacts of receiving results varied and included relief, peace of mind, reduced guilt, disappointment, fear, frustration, stress, blame, and guilt. Results varied widely, making it hard to compare studies; one clear outcome is that more research with and for autistic people is needed, including children when possible.

## Introduction

Clinical guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that all families with an autistic1 child be offered “genetic evaluation” as part of an etiological workup.2 Research on genetic contributions to autism (together with research on environmental causes) has in recent years constituted the second largest portion of over $400 million spent on autism research annually in the United States.3 As a result, researchers are increasingly offering autism-related genetic information to participants.4,5 The ongoing Simons Foundation Powering Autism Research for Knowledge (SPARK) study, for instance, has enrolled over 390,000 people diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and their biological family members, with the goal of sequencing their genomes and returning the results to them.6 Investment in autism-related genetic testing is also growing in the commercial sector.7

Autism-related genetic testing may be offered to autistic adolescents and adults, parents of infants and children, or prospective parents who are planning to become or already are pregnant, to parents of infants and children, or to autistic adolescents and adults. Some tests are offered as part of a research study, while others are offered in clinical care. Some autism-related genetic tests use microarray technology while others employ exome or genome sequencing. The different testing technologies can identify copy-number variants or high-penetrance single-gene variants, with the rate of diagnostic findings ranging from 5–10% for microarrays to 15–20% for exome sequencing.8

As autism-related genetic testing has grown, so have relevant ethical and equity challenges. For example, because autism-related genetic testing can facilitate access to educational and other institutional supports, racialized inequities in testing access may compound disadvantages.9,10 Those concerns suggest the need for broader access to genetic testing for families from underserved communities. However, from an alternate perspective, many autistic people and their advocates oppose genetic testing, concerned that it focuses attention on the cause of autism rather than accepting autistic people and that the results will facilitate the avoidance or termination of pregnancies with a heightened likelihood of producing a child with autism.11

In addition to these ethical considerations, the decision about whether to test will depend in part on the risk/benefit ratio of testing, including the ways in which the results may affect autistic people and their family members. In light of such concerns, it is critical to assess not only attitudes toward testing but also the impacts of receiving test results on autistic people and their relatives. Such impacts could include effects on mental health or well-being, such as increased depression or anxiety, emotional impacts such as increased worry or increased optimism, or social impacts such as increased access to educational support. Previous reviews of the psychosocial impacts of returning genetic testing results, both in general12–17 and in specific research or clinical contexts18–24, have generally found transitory distress and limited behavioral change following receipt of results. Although a few reviews have focused on autism,24–26 none to date has focused on the impact of autism-related genetic test results on autistic people, parents, and prospective parents. This systematic review addresses that gap.

## Methods

This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021258842) and followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) reporting guidelines (Figure).27

We analyzed the primary research and review literatures on the psychosocial impacts of genetic testing to derive a list of 90 search terms covering autism, genetic testing, and the psychosocial or behavioral impacts of test results (Table S1, available online).

We included only English-language results of peer-reviewed human subjects research published on or after the launch of the Human Genome Project (1990). We excluded articles that only investigated participants’ perceptions of autism-related genetic testing. We included articles that returned results of such testing or that asked participants to imagine receiving such results (“hypothetical” studies). Studies in the latter group asked, for example, how receiving a positive prenatal result would impact prenatal decision making and were not restricted to technologies already in use. We excluded articles with fewer than 5 participants for qualitative studies or fewer than 20 participants for quantitative studies. We did not include studies of genetic syndromes, such as Fragile X syndrome, which include autism as one of several features of the condition. Studies of the impacts of genetic testing for such syndromes do not isolate the impact of receiving autism-related results from the impact of receiving results related to the syndrome overall.

We searched title and abstract fields in MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science Core Collection, Sociological Index, and Scopus three times between June 26, 2021, and October 27, 2024. In addition, we examined articles included or cited in similar systematic reviews12–15,18,19,22–26 and articles citing each of the articles included at the full-text stage. We also searched Google Scholar for 43 researchers known to be active in this area. Results were imported into Covidence systematic review software.28 After removing duplicates, two pairs of reviewers (AU1and AU4; AU2 and AU3) independently screened titles and abstracts, then full texts of the remaining articles (Figure). Reviewer discussion addressed any disagreement. Article data were extracted (Table S2, available online) and analyzed for study characteristics, article findings, and conclusions and recommendations (Table S3, available online). Analysis was discussed in detail by AU2, AU1, and AU3 and reviewed by all co-authors. Two reviewers (AU2 and AU3) independently assessed eligible articles using the Quality Appraisal for Diverse Studies (QuADS) tool (Table S4, available online).29 This tool was selected for its ability to evaluate diverse research methodologies, including qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies. Each criterion was scored on a 4-point scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 3 (complete). Author discussion resolved scoring discrepancies. In accordance with QuADS guidance, there was no cut-off score. Given the emerging nature of this research area, we adopted this inclusive approach to capture the breadth of available evidence while acknowledging variations in methodological rigor.

## Results

In total, authors screened and assessed 3,606 relevant articles. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria (Figure), 22 articles reporting the experiences of 3,983 individuals in 17 studies were reviewed.

### Study Characteristics

Among the 22 articles that met the final inclusion criteria (Table 1), 17 focused on parents/caregivers of autistic children, three on the prenatal context, and two on autistic adults. Of the 16 studies that reported race/ethnicity of participants, all but two (C,M) had over 70% white samples. All but two articles (I,U) reported on the sex, gender, and/or parental role of participants, with the majority being female, women, and/or mothers. Although one study (H) surveyed parents and autistic adolescents and adults, psychosocial impact data were reported only for the parent group.

Three articles compared experiences of participants who had received results with those who had not, but separately reported additional results for the tested group (A,B,E). Most articles (n=18) focused exclusively on genetic testing related to autism, while four considered the impact of results related to autism alongside other conditions (G,P-R).

Article methods included qualitative interviews (n=9), surveys (n=8), and combinations of interviews, surveys, and medical record reviews (n=5). Most articles (n=18) reported on the impacts of receiving actual genetic test results, while four assessed the impacts of hypothetical return-of-results scenarios (A,C,D,Q). In the articles reporting the impacts of actual test results, the most common method of genetic testing was chromosomal microarray (CMA; n=6) (F,G,I,N,O,R). Five articles from two studies reported on the return of whole genome and/or exome sequencing results (J-L,S,T), four articles considered results from various types of genetic testing (H,M,P,V), and three did not specify the testing approach (B,E,U). Five articles from two studies differentiated between de novo and inherited findings (J-L,R,T). Of the four hypothetical studies, none specified the test type, though one contextualized findings in light of the emergence of polygenic scores (A) and another in light of CMA (D). None of the included studies specifically compared psychosocial impacts between different genetic testing technologies (e.g., CMA versus whole exome sequencing). Additionally, heterogeneity in study designs, assessment methods, reporting formats, and outcome measures across studies prevented meaningful analysis of whether impacts varied systematically by testing methodology.

Most articles (n=15) were retrospective. One mixed retrospective/prospective cohort study surveyed parents who had requested testing for an autistic child (pretest group) or already received results (posttest group) (M). Two articles collected data at multiple time points, using either a six-month pre–post design (S) or a 12-month longitudinal design with baseline, one-month, and twelve-month follow-up assessments (T).

We used the QuADS appraisal tool to assess q uality.29 Designed for multi- and mixed-methods health services research, QuADS provides a percentage score across a range of criteria. Scores ranged from 69% to 95%, with an average of 81% (see Supplement 4). Though articles scoring below 70% are sometimes excluded from systematic reviews, we kept the lowest-scoring article given the emergent nature of the field. Articles scored highest on stating clear research aims and choosing appropriate methods of analysis and lowest on considering relevant research stakeholders.

### Article Findings

Our analysis focuses on findings directly related to the psychosocial impacts of receiving genetic test results and identifies six sub-categories covering cognitive, emotional, and behavioral impacts (Table 2). Where articles included a mix of participants who had and had not undergone testing, we report disaggregated results whenever possible.

#### Perceived benefits, risks, and limitations of testing

Nineteen studies explored participants’ perceptions of benefits, risks, and limitations of genetic testing for autism (A-E,G,I-V). Thirteen studies directly asked participants about perceived benefits and limitations of testing (B,E,H,I,L-V), while seven analyzed participants’ reasons for undergoing or forgoing testing (A,C,H,I,M,U,V) and twelve examined impacts after receiving results (B,E,H,I,L-V). Eight studies quantitatively characterized participants’ views (C,D,H,M,U,V), while eleven presented primarily qualitative findings or did not quantify the prevalence of specific perceptions (A,G,F,I-O,R).

Studies identified several perceived benefits of testing, the most frequently cited of which were obtaining causal explanations (C,K,L,N,T-V), improving understanding of autism (I,K,L,M,U), and informing medical management (I,K,L,M,U). Seven studies reported benefits related to reproductive decision-making (C,D,E,I-K,M) and contributing to research (C,E,I,K,T-V).

Perceived risks and limitations included uncertainty in results (F,I,N,T), financial costs (B,E,U), and concerns about discrimination (A,B,D,E). Three studies reported participants questioning testing’s value or utility (A,C,U). One study found 71.4% of those declining testing cited lack of value as their primary reason, while half of those who completed testing reported that it wasn’t useful (U). Two studies reported concerns specific to prenatal contexts, including implications for pregnancy termination decisions (C,D).

Two studies found anticipated benefits before testing were consistently higher than reported benefits after receiving results (M,U). One study noted that the proportion of parents who rated understanding test capabilities and limitations as important (89.6%) contrasted sharply with the proportion of parents (40%) who reported receiving adequate information about testing (H).

#### Understanding of the genetic test results

Parents sometimes expected genetic testing to provide clarity regarding the underlying cause of their child’s autism and experienced confusion when results did not resolve uncertainty surrounding etiology and prognosis (F,G,U).

Participants’ understandings of test results were sometimes inconsistent with scientific explanations, with seven articles reporting that parents interpreted results through preexisting ideas about autism and genetics (F,J,N,O,R,T); two reporting modest, decreasing or erroneous understandings of reproductive implications (K,T); and at least one article reporting enduring misconceptions despite education to the contrary (O).

Six articles reported that genetic testing results led parents to view their child’s autism as more definitive, permanent, or severe than previously understood (H,K,L,N,O,T). This change was especially true for parents who were informed of causal variants. Conversely, some parents who received results not indicating a causal variant, or results for inherited (as opposed to de novo) causal variants, were more optimistic about their child’s prognosis (O,R,T). One study (H) found a negative correlation between confusion over results and self-described adequacy of information, but a positive correlation between confusion over results and having few to no questions.

#### Attitudes toward testing

The two studies of autistic persons reported opposition to testing without the autistic person’s consent (B,E), and three studies in total reported negative attitudes toward the use of genetic information to search for a cure or for prenatal testing followed by abortion (A,B,E). Where studies asked parents about satisfaction with the testing experience, two articles found high (>80%) satisfaction (P,S), while the majority reported low (< 51%) (F-H,U) or moderate (51%–80%) satisfaction (C,D,N,V), which was often highly variable within studies.

Parents were disappointed when testing fell short of their expectations, most commonly when tests failed to provide a definitive etiological explanation, an improved understanding of their child’s condition, a prognosis, or practical benefits for the child’s care, such as educational supports. Parents who received results indicating a causal variant were generally more likely to view testing as helpful than parents who did not (F,G,I,N,S,T), although parents generally experienced continued uncertainty (F,G,I,O,Q,R-T). In some cases, a lack of adequate support or information from healthcare professionals contributed to negative attitudes toward testing (F,I,V).

#### Satisfaction with support from providers

While some parents reported receiving adequate (U) or good (P) care, many more said that their information needs were unmet and identified gaps in instruction, counseling, and health guidelines (F,H,S,V) Some parents reported being under- or uninformed about genetics, the testing process, and results’ relevance to diagnosis and life-long care. A survey of autistic adults, including some who had received genetic testing, reported over 78% agreed that autistic persons would benefit from contact with a genetic counselor in certain situations (E).

#### Psychosocial impacts of receiving test results

In one study, most autistic persons who had undergone genetic testing reported that they did not gain more diagnostic certainty, or better understand why they were autistic, nor did they gain access to more supports or more acceptance from family (B). However, the other study involving autistic adults reported that most of those who had undergone genetic testing thought that testing did help them receive or confirm their diagnosis and access specific treatments, and that it provided information about themselves (E). Some parents who received results identifying a causal variant experienced relief and peace of mind due to finally having an etiological explanation or knowing that their own genetics or parenting were not to blame (G,H,I,K,M,N,Q,T). Reduced self-blame was particularly noted where a de novo variant was identified (J,L,T). However, two studies noted that some parents who received such results experienced blame and guilt, although neither article quantified how many parents reported these impacts or compared them to positive reactions (N,Q).

Some parents who did not receive results indicating a causal variant also experienced relief (F,G,N,R). However, parents who received uninformative results were more commonly disappointed, leading to frustration, fear, and stress (F,G,I,R,Q). Regardless of the type of result received, many parents experienced stress or anxiety due to residual uncertainty regarding the meaning and actionability of results (F,G,L,M,R,T).

Ten articles noted behavioral impacts of results such as altered care plans, greater empowerment in coordinating care and educational support, increased information-seeking, preparation for the birth of an autistic child, or changes in family planning (A,E,G,J-L,N,R-T). Parents in three studies noted that receiving results allowed them to connect with support (M,N,R). In seven articles, parents reported being more patient with and accepting of their child’s behavior (K,N-P,T,V), or in the case of hypothetical results, predicting that they would be more patient or accepting (A).

Few studies assessed the degree of psychosocial impacts. Many stated that participants felt “some” relief, anxiety, guilt, or similar emotion or did not have a one-sided experience (e.g., parents who felt disappointed still thought it best to be more informed). In four articles, most participants stated they would likely undergo autism-related genetic testing for a future child (C-D,S), while one article reported that the majority would not (despite 80% of parents reporting that the results were important to them) (I). Another article reported significant concern from parents that polygenic prediction of autism at birth would cause more harm than good (A). Interestingly, many participants who reported limited satisfaction or usefulness nevertheless said it was advantageous to be more informed (F,I,Q). In three articles, when asked, most parents said they would at least cautiously recommend testing to other parents of autistic children (H,M,V).

#### Impact on decisions to terminate or continue pregnancies

All three prenatal studies investigated the real or imagined impact of genetic test results on pregnancy termination decisions. Two studies presented hypothetical results indicating a causal variant, with 71% (C) and 53% (D) of parents predicting that they would terminate the pregnancy. The single article on actual decisions found that 67% (R) of women who received results of a causal variant terminated their pregnancies.

Reasons for continuing pregnancies in which the fetus had a causal variant included: the bond with existing autistic children, concerns about limitations of the prenatal test, and religious beliefs. Reasons for ending such pregnancies included perceived stigma and perceived burden on the affected child, family, and society.

#### Autistic persons’ overall experiences and interest in testing

The two articles reporting autistic adults’ experiences and interest in testing yielded divergent findings. One study of autistic adults found that most who had undergone testing felt positive about testing, would pursue testing in the future for their children, and would recommend it for other autistic people (E). But the other article reported that those who had undergone testing varied greatly in their enthusiasm and reported few benefits (B). In the latter study, more than half of the larger cohort surveyed (a mix of individuals who had and had not undergone testing) would not have wanted testing as a child and would not want their own children to receive testing.

### Recommendations of Included Articles

All articles made recommendations related to clinical practice or future research. Several articles addressed societal and policy issues. We identified four main categories of recommendations (Table 3).

#### Access to genetic testing

Thirteen articles concluded that genetic testing was beneficial or valuable, with twelve recommending that parents be offered genetic testing (C,F-M,P,U,V). One study of parents stressed harms and benefits (A), while the two studies that included autistic adults who had received genetic testing leaned in favor of waiting for testing until the autistic person can consent (B,E). Levels of enthusiasm for testing varied. One article concluded that it is “critical for healthcare providers to be more proactive in providing ASD genetic testing information to all parents” of autistic children (V, p4,829). In contrast, another article urged counselors to help parents understand “the potential and future opinions of their autistic children regarding genetic testing… [and] the need for autonomy in making a decision about testing” (E, p12). Yet other articles de-emphasized access to genetic testing when compared to the other service and support needs of autistic people and their families (A,E,K).

#### Access to pre- and post-test education and counseling

All but two articles (A,S) emphasized the importance of helping parents and prospective parents understand the goals and limitations of genetic testing and the meaning of individual results. Several stressed the importance of pre-test counseling to help participants develop realistic expectations of testing, while other articles emphasized the value of support when parents or prospective parents receive uncertain results.

#### Education, training, and resources for health professionals

Eight articles suggested that providers be offered additional education, training, or resources (B,C,F,K,Q,R,S,V). One recommended that discussion of results involve staff experienced with autistic children (F), while another suggested a new kind of patient-facing testing report developed with the help of patients (S). Two articles stressed the range of issues that clinicians should be prepared to address with autistic patients and their families (P,O).

#### Further research on psychosocial impacts

All but three articles (F,H,S) concluded that additional research is needed to elucidate the psychosocial impacts of genetic testing. Several articles identified the need for larger and more diverse samples, including studying the impact of results on autistic people themselves.

## Discussion

This systematic review identified 22 articles assessing the psychosocial impacts of autism-related genetic testing. Most participants were prospective or current parents who received actual or hypothetical results. Some articles focused only on autism, while others also covered other conditions. Three conclusions emerged from synthetic analysis:

- The impacts on parents and prospective parents of receiving autism-related genetic testing results appear mixed in valence and relatively modest in effect; nevertheless, there is a clear need for expectation setting and enhanced educational support for clinicians, patients, and families.

Although most parents and prospective parents welcomed autism-related genetic testing, they experienced a mix of positive and negative impacts. Emotionally, results led to feelings of relief, including reduced guilt, and sometimes improved patience with and understanding of their child’s behaviors. However, some parents or prospective parents who expected definitive answers were quite disappointed to receive results not indicating a causal variant, leading many authors to recommend attention to pre- and post-test counseling, including enhanced education, training, and resources for providers. Clinicians, including psychiatrists, psychologists, and genetic counselors, should be aware that although genetic testing is likely becoming more familiar to the public due to the availability of direct-to-consumer genetics and increased use in medical care, 80% of autism cases do not have causal variants currently identifiable by genetic testing.8 Prospective and current parents may thus need help forming realistic expectations of genetic testing and understanding the meaning and potential utility of their results. If expectations are more realistic and overall understanding is improved, the psychosocial impacts of autism-related genetic testing might differ from those observed in this review. For instance, realistic expectations of testing might result in less disappointment when genetic testing does not return a result or where the result is uncertain. Relatedly, the link between understanding of results and negative psychosocial impacts was underexplored.

In addition, given recent articles reporting that autistic people are opposed to or concerned about genetic testing without the consent or involvement of the autistic person, clinicians may need to help parents understand this concern and, depending on the age and capacity of the child, support the child to participate in decisions about testing. Researchers designing studies and healthcare providers integrating testing into clinical care should plan to address these counseling and training needs. Whether or how these needs are greater or otherwise different for autism compared to other conditions warrants future study.

- While many articles favor offering genetic testing, some newer articles report concerns among some autistic people and some parents of autistic people that genetic testing and genetic research might harm them or their community, illustrating the importance of considering the broader societal context in which testing takes place when issuing recommendations.

Despite finding mixed impacts of returning genetic test results, many of the included articles concluded by emphasizing the benefits of and calling for increased availability of autism-related genetic testing. Some of the newer articles, however, explicitly considered the inequitable healthcare and social support landscapes of their research contexts (A,B,E,J). Additionally, it was in newer studies that participants voiced more systemic concerns, for example about representation of autistic children and adults in research design and agenda setting and the possibility for genetics research to lead to the eradication of autistic people. In practice settings, clinicians could inform parents of the mixed reaction to genetic testing among some members of the autistic community so that parents understand more about how testing might be perceived by others and, one day, by their child. Finally, while some articles recognized the relevance of disparities generally (C,D,F,V), few explicitly investigated disparities in access to testing due to rurality, race, socioeconomic status, or insurance status. These disparities should be a focus of future research.

- Future research should assess the impacts of genetic testing on autistic people and include more diverse study populations.

Nearly all included articles examined the impacts of genetic testing on parents or prospective parents. Only two reported the impacts of autism-related genetic testing on people who identify as autistic and/or have an ASD diagnosis (B,E). Although these two articles reported different results, together they suggest that research including autistic people can yield insights that differ from the insights gained from studies focused on parents and prospective parents. One of these articles characterized the differences between the motivations of clinicians and parents and the experiences of autistic adults around genetic testing as a “disconnect” and a “tension” that “urgently requires dialog” (B, p8). Facilitating research with autistic participants can require special considerations, but stakeholders have identified steps to improve participants’ experiences.51 Research co-design, which involves people from the target population meaningfully participating in, designing, and sometimes co-leading research projects,52 has been shown to improve outcomes and participation in autism research, leading to greater participant investment in the research process53 and higher engagement and psychosocial benefits for participants.54 The two studies of autistic adults included in this review (B,E), both of which included autistic members in the research team, may serve as models for future research, as may other studies with autistic participants that did not meet our inclusion criteria but demonstrate inclusive approaches.55

Also needed are larger and more demographically diverse studies that expand the range of findings and counter selection bias. Research that focuses explicitly on the experiences of Black and multiracial parents of autistic children, for example, identifies racialized provider behaviors and differences in disability knowledge and attitudes that are essential for contextualizing diagnostic experiences, considerations absent in most studies.56 Recent scholarship has indicated that without multiply diverse participant pools and autistic persons as co-researchers, studies’ findings, conclusions, and recommendations—as well as the policies they influence—are less likely to reflect the needs and experiences of many autistic people and their families.57,58

Longitudinal research should also be pursued. Among the articles included here, Wynn et al.’s (T) and Williams et al.’s (S) pre–post designs were the longest in duration (12 months and 3–6-plus months, respectively). Longitudinal research over several years could assess how autism-related genetic test results returned during pregnancy, early childhood, childhood, or adulthood impact autistic people, parents, and their relationships over time. As children become adults and develop their identities, along with navigating the worlds of education, health and life insurance, employment, and parenting, genetic test results may shape their lives in ways not well captured by short-duration studies.

### Limitations of this systematic review

We limited searches to articles that included “autism” or “Asperger*” in the title or abstract and excluded studies of specific genetic variations or conditions with autism as part of the phenotype, such as the 22q.11 deletion or Fragile X syndrome. A future review might compare the impacts of autism-related genetic testing and genetic testing for syndromes in which autism is one feature.

Perhaps because this systematic review examines a nascent line of research, we encountered substantial heterogeneity in research populations, methods, quality, terminology, and target literatures. This heterogeneity, combined with design limitations addressed above and small sample sizes in some studies, made it challenging to draw cross-cutting conclusions about the impacts of receiving autism genetic results. For the same reason, while it would be valuable to characterize the impact of knowledge level or changes over time in the experiences of families undergoing autism-related genetic testing, the present body of evidence can only hint at possible directions. As more research is conducted in this area, particularly including impacts on autistic people themselves, firmer conclusions may be possible.

## Conclusions

In this systematic review, we identified 22 articles from 17 studies reporting the psychosocial impacts of autism-related genetic testing. Two reported impacts on autistic adults, but the vast majority focused on current and prospective parents. Impacts appeared mixed in valence and relatively modest overall, findings that are broadly in line with other return-of-results research for complex genetic conditions.59 However, specific concerns were raised in some articles about genetic testing of children without their consent and the potential for autism genetics research to stigmatize autistic people and lead to increased termination of affected pregnancies. Clinicians should be aware of these concerns and able to help parents understand and weigh them in their decision-making. Where appropriate, clinicians could assist parents to involve autistic children in testing decisions. Most studies lacked participant diversity, were not longitudinal, and did not address the impact of receiving genetic testing results on autistic people, indicating significant gaps in the literature.
